# guard cannot read. Both reach a database; neither is visible to a rule that
# reads one segment at a time.

# does not exist, so they take the textual path on every machine — which is the
# path CI took for the whole root, where the guard refused its own scratchpad.

# `cd` succeeds and the answer comes from the filesystem rather than from the
# text. The traversal case above lands on /Users and a different section catches
# it either way, so it pins nothing here. This one lands in /private/tmp, which

# than any word added to it: a `git` at the head exempted the whole command,
# `segments()` cut inline interpreter code into pieces before it was read, and a
# wrapper flag's value was read as the verb.
# The verb, spelled the ways bash accepts and this used to compare literally.
# `rm -rf ~/dev` was refused and `\rm -rf ~/dev` was not — and a backslash is
# what people type to step around an `rm -i` alias, so the delete boundary was
# one keystroke deep. The quoted forms are the same defect, and `${IFS}` is a
# fourth: the whole thing is one whitespace-free token, whose basename was `dev`.
# The limit that stays: until the shell expands it, the verb is genuinely
# unknown, and guessing which command a variable holds is not something a string
# matcher can do. Written down here rather than discovered by the next person.
# Container execution is a wrapper with one extra word. Reported by a host
# project that walked around its own hook this way; `rm -rf` was refused and
# `docker exec pg rm -rf` was not, which took every rule in the file with it
# rather than the delete boundary alone.
# And the other direction, which is what stops the fix from becoming "refuse
# every container command". The name after `exec` is skipped once and only after
# `exec`, so ordinary subcommands still read as themselves.
# `docker run` with a bind mount is not covered, and that is a decision rather
# than an omission. Three things would have to be true to cover it, and the
# One: parse the mount grammar. A bind mount is spelled at least eight ways —
# target=/c`, the same keys as src/dst, in any order — and two of the spellings
# threaten nothing (`-v name:/c` is a named volume, `-v /c` is anonymous), so
# telling them apart is part of the job.
# Two: map the container path back. Knowing `/x` is `/Users/someone` is what
# makes `rm -rf /x/dev` the refusable thing, and that means modelling the
# container filesystem rather than matching a string. This guard also reads the
# command before the shell expands it, so `-v $PWD:/app` is four literal
# characters here and the shell alone knows where they point.
# Three, and this is the one that ends it: the command need not be in the line
# at all. See the second case below. What an image does on start is known only
# The cheap heuristic — a bind mount plus the word `rm` somewhere — dies on
# `--rm`, which is the most common flag `docker run` takes and appears in
# almost every real invocation. A guard that refuses `docker run --rm -v
# $PWD:/app node npm test` teaches people to work around it everywhere else.
# No verb anywhere in the line. Nothing a string matcher can reach: the deletion
# is inside the image. This case is here so the limit is a claim in the corpus
# rather than a silence, the way `$r -rf` above is.
# A package manager running a command is the same wrapper, from the same report.
# After `docker exec` comes a container name; after `pnpm exec` comes the command

# keep reading as `npm`, and it did become `run` in the first draft of this.
# `dlx` runs a package, and what a package does is not in the command line — the
